The '''2003–04 FA Premier League''' (known as the '''FA [[Barclaycard]] Premiership''') was the 12th season of the [[Premier League]]. [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] were crowned champions ending the season [[The Invincibles (English football)|without a single defeat]] – the first team ever to do so in a 38–game league season.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.premierleague.com/pl30/the-invincibles|title=The Invincibles Team of Arsenal 2003/04 &#124; PL30|website=Premierleague.com|access-date=24 June 2026|archive-date=24 May 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250524210412/https://www.premierleague.com/pl30/the-invincibles|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] finished second to Arsenal.

==Season summary==
Having qualified for the Champions League the previous season, Chelsea were bolstered by a £100&nbsp;million outlay on world-class players, a spree funded by the extensive financial resources of their new owner [[Roman Abramovich]]. Manchester United's attack was as strong as ever thanks to free-scoring [[Ruud van Nistelrooy]], but the midfield was weakened following the £25&nbsp;million pre-season sale of [[David Beckham]] to [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]], and the centre of defence suffered a more severe setback after [[Rio Ferdinand]] was ruled out for the final four months of the season after being found guilty of the "failure or refusal to take a drugs test". The case of Rio Ferdinand started a debate about punishments relating to drug testing in football, with there being differing views on whether the punishment was too harsh or too lenient. Ferdinand's club sought to make direct comparisons with an earlier case of Manchester City reserve player who had in fact committed a lesser drug testing offence and as a result escaped with only a fine.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/news/motive-is-always-considered-in-deciding-guilt-576995.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220501/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/news/motive-is-always-considered-in-deciding-guilt-576995.html |archive-date=1 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live | work=The Independent | location=London | title=Motive is always considered in deciding guilt | first=Nick | last=Harris | date=18 December 2003 | access-date=21 April 2010 }}{{cbignore}}{{Dead link|date=August 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> [[Manchester City F.C.|City]] themselves had just moved from [[Maine Road]] to the [[City of Manchester Stadium]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mcfc.co.uk/the-club/club-history|title=Club History|publisher=Manchester City Football Club|access-date=16 February 2013|archive-date=16 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160516024406/http://www.mcfc.co.uk/the-club/club-history|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Arsenal, meanwhile, had only signed German goalkeeper [[Jens Lehmann]] in the 2003 close season, but French striker [[Thierry Henry]] was instrumental in Arsenal's success. Away from the Premier League, [[Arsène Wenger]]'s team suffered disappointment in the cup competitions; they were knocked-out by [[2003–04 Football League Cup|League Cup]] eventual winners Middlesbrough in the semi-finals, lost their grip on the [[2003–04 FA Cup|FA Cup]] (which they held for two consecutive seasons) after being defeated by eventual winners Manchester United in the semi-finals, and were knocked out of the [[2003–04 UEFA Champions League|Champions League]] quarter-finals by Chelsea 3–2 on aggregate. These blows in the FA Cup and Champions League came within a few days of each other, and it was thought that Arsenal might squander their lead of the Premier League for the second successive season, but Arsenal easily defeated [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] only days later.

In the end, Wenger led the North-London club to a first [[The Invincibles (English football)|undefeated season]], solidifying his managerial legacy and longevity to the Arsenal fanbase as they finished the season with 26 wins, 12 draws, 0 defeats, and 90 points, winning the title with an 11-point margin over [[Claudio Ranieri]]'s Chelsea. [[Thierry Henry]] proved decisive in the critical moments, inspiring comebacks against close rivals Liverpool and Chelsea, including a hat-trick to seal a 4–2 win having been 2–1 down.

The relegation spots were occupied by three teams bracketed together on 33 points. [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolves]] and [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] followed the trend of many other newly promoted Premier League clubs and were relegated just one season after reaching the top division. For Leicester City, they would not return to the top flight for another [[2014-15 Premier League|10 years]] and became the league champions for the first time ever in their history just a season later, whilst Wolves were promoted back to the top flight in [[2009–10 Premier League|2009]] and slipped down again [[2011–12 Premier League|3 years]] later. The other relegation place went to [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]], whose playing fortunes had dipped in the past two seasons after [[David O'Leary]] was sacked as manager and club debts had risen so high that many star players had to be sold. As a result, Leeds were relegated from the Premier League after 14 years of top division football – just three seasons after they had reached the Champions League semifinals - and they would not return for another [[2020–21 Premier League|16 years]], during which time they suffered a further relegation to the [[EFL League One|third tier]] in [[2006-07 Football League Championship|2007]] and came close towards going out of business in the process.

In his third season as Middlesbrough manager, [[Steve McClaren]] guided the Teessiders to their first ever major trophy – sealed with a 2–1 win over [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]] in the [[EFL Cup|League Cup]] final. McClaren was also the first English manager to win a major trophy since Brian Little guided [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] to League Cup success in 1996. He was also the first manager to take Middlesbrough into European competition – they would be competing in the 2004–05 [[UEFA Cup]].

==Teams==
Twenty teams competed in the league&nbsp;– the top seventeen teams from the previous season and the three teams promoted from the [[2002–03 Football League First Division|First Division]]. The promoted teams were [[Portsmouth F.C.|Portsmouth]], [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] and [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolverhampton Wanderers]], returning to the top flight after an absence of fifteen, one and nineteen years respectively. This was also both Portsmouth's and Wolverhampton Wanderers' first season in the Premier League. They replaced [[West Ham United F.C.|West Ham United]], [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] and [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]], who were relegated to the [[2003–04 Football League First Division|First Division]] after spending time in the top flight for ten, one and four years respectively.

*Most wins – [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] (26)
*Fewest wins – [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] (6)
*Most draws – [[Newcastle United F.C.|Newcastle United]] (17)
*Fewest draws – [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] and [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] (6)
*Most losses – [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] (21)
*Fewest losses – [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] (0)
*Most goals scored – [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] (73)
*Fewest goals scored – [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolverhampton Wanderers]] (38)
*Most goals conceded – [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] (79)
*Fewest goals conceded – [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] (26)
